newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Sarajevo church bomb exposes Moslem-Croat tension.
newsitem.headline: Sarajevo church bomb exposes Moslem-Croat tension.

text.p: Bosnian authorities suspended four policemen on Tuesday pending an investigation into the bombing of a Roman Catholic church in Sarajevo they were supposed to be guarding.
The announcement came on state media hours after a bomb went off at the back door of Saint Joseph's church just after one a.m. (midnight GMT), shattering windows in two residential buildings nearby.
No one was injured in the blast, only 20 metres (yards) from a police station.

The interior ministry for the Sarajevo area said in a statement that it was investigating the explosion and pledged to "correct possible mistakes and determine the responsibility of people who could have stopped the incident".
The ministry said four police officers assigned to guard the church on Monday night had been suspended until the investigation was completed.
The announcement came after the Croatian government called on Bosnian Moslem authorities to take forceful action to halt attacks on Catholic property.

Tuesday's explosion was the latest in a series of attacks on Catholic churches and buildings in Bosnia's troubled Moslem-Croat Federation. Tensions have been running high after a shooting incident in the southern town of Mostar last month.

The federation was plunged into crisis after Croat police, some in plain clothes, opened fire on Moslems trying to visit a cemetery in Croat-held western Mostar. One Moslem man was shot dead in the February 10 incident.
A hand grenade was thrown at another Roman Catholic church and a convent in Sarajevo last week. In central Bosnia, a bomb was planted at a church.

Hido Biscevic, an aide to the Croatian foreign minister, conveyed his dismay over the latest incident in talks with the Bosnian ambassador to Croatia, Kasim Trnka, the Croatian news agency HINA reported.
"Biscevic protested most strongly against the latest attack at the church of Saint Joseph," HINA reported.

Croatia was indignant that those who had committed acts of violence had not been brought to justice, and it expected more forceful action "particularly in the light of the forthcoming visit of Pope John Paul to Sarajevo," he was quoted as saying.
The Pope had to cancel a planned wartime visit to Sarajevo in 1994 when Serb forces laying siege to the city refused to guarantee his safety.
The Catholic church information office for the scheduled papal visit had received threatening phone calls and had to shut down for a day, Bosnian newspapers reported last week.
The main Moslem party, the Party of Democratic Action (SDA), said it "most strongly condemns these terrorist acts" and urged authorities to arrest those who had attacked Catholic buildings.
Bosnian Moslem leaders had pledged to step up security around Catholic churches and other buildings before Tuesday's bombing.
Moslems and Croats fought a vicious 10-month war in 1993-94 before agreeing to form a federation under U.S. pressure. The federation and a Serb territory comprise peacetime Bosnia.
